newsitem.title: FRANCE: Early election rumours gain ground in France.
newsitem.headline: Early election rumours gain ground in France.

text.p: French politicians on Friday prepared for a possible early general election amid strong rumours President Jacques Chirac might call a June poll to renew his centre-right majority and clear the decks for a crucial year in European integration.

The Paris stock market's CAC 40 index tumbled 2.59 percent on fears of a period of political uncertainty and perhaps a new round of fiscal austerity to help France qualify for the European Union's planned single currency. French bonds and the franc also weakened.

"Dissolving (parliament) looks the most likely possibility, but nothing is ruled out. The president faces a difficult decision that he has to make on his own," said Michel Pericard, head of Chirac's RPR Gaullist party in the National Assembly.
The National Assembly's five-year term expires in March 1998. Speculation of an early election has gained ground over rumours that Chirac may be considering a less dramatic cabinet reshuffle.
"I expect a dissolution before Thursday," said RPR deputy Jean-Yves Chamard. "My posters are ordered and my electoral newspaper is coming out next week."
The Assembly, discussing a bill on poverty, was much emptier than usual on Friday as most deputies hurried back to their constituencies for a weekend of work.

Education Minister Francois Bayrou denied reports quoting him as saying that Chirac would announce a decision next Thursday, following the weekly Wednesday cabinet meeting. "There is only one person who knows what he's going to say and when he's going to say it. That's the president," he told Reuters.

Ignoring the election fever gripping the country, Chirac kept reporters guessing as he toured the Louvre museum in Paris. "It will be beautiful," was his only comment. He was referring to work under way to extend the museum.
Commentators singled out June 1 and 8 as the most likely
dates for a two-stage election, after Chirac returns on May 21 from a trip to China and before he attends the June 15 European Union summit in Amsterdam.

Elections have to be held between 20 and 40 days after the assembly is dissolved. That means Chirac could not announce a dissolution of parliament and an election for June 1 before the middle of next week because it is still more than 40 days away.

The afternoon daily newspaper Le Monde said Prime Minister Alain Juppe and allies believed they had convinced Chirac to risk an early election to secure a renewed centre-right majority for the rest of his seven-year term, which expires in 2002.

Roland Cayrol of the CSA polling institute said that Chirac would be taking a huge risk. He said many people were undecided -- recent opinion polls have predicted a close battle but differed on whether the centre-right or the left would win.
And Cayrol asked: "What would Chirac's legitimacy be?" if opposition Socialist leader Lionel Jospin became prime minister for the next five years in a public vote that snubbed Chirac.

The government won 80 percent of seats in the Assembly four years ago, but its public support has slumped over the past 16 months because of budget austerity to qualify for the single EU currency and persistent record unemployment.
Analysts said Chirac may be tempted to seize on a slight brightening of economic prospects and the government's popularity to try to catch the Left unprepared.

If he called a vote, he was expected to argue that it was needed to prepare for a vital year of European integration. The European Union is due to decide early in 1998 which countries attain predetermined criteria to join the single currency due for launch in 1999.
Finance Minister Jean Arthuis denied reports that the government was facing problems in meeting Maastricht treaty budget criteria and so might be forced to introduce unpopular spending cuts.

"I'd like to say to you, and repeat to you, that public spending is under control and the government will meet the three percent target," Arthuis said, adding he had confidence in the government's growth and public deficit forecasts.
A Lyon printer said he had tens of tonnes of paper delivered days ago in anticipation for printing campaign propaganda.
